categories.howToSpot: Built around the current year's digits, with soaps standing in for zeros. Spot it when you're holding 2s and soaps.
categories.requires: a year hand is built from the year's digits, with soaps for zeros, so it wants 2s and soaps rather than a spread of numbers

categories.howToSpot: Only even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8). Every odd tile in your hand is dead weight for this section.
categories.requires: an evens hand uses only 2s, 4s, 6s and 8s for its numbers, so look for it when those four numbers fill the rack

categories.howToSpot: The same number collected across different suits. Spot it when one number keeps showing up in two or three suits at once.
categories.requires: like numbers means the same number across different suits, so a rack spread across several numbers is not it

categories.howToSpot: Needs five of a kind, and only four of each tile exist, so quints are impossible without jokers. Only chase these when you're joker-rich.
categories.requires: quints need five of a kind, which is impossible without jokers, so this is a joker question before it is a number question

categories.howToSpot: Numbers that step up in order, like 4-5-6-7. Unless a line's note names its numbers, a run can start on any number, so a deal with numbers in a row can fit more than one line.
categories.requires: a run needs numbers stepping up in order with no gaps, which always mixes odd and even

categories.howToSpot: Only odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7, 9). The mirror image of 2468, with one more number to build from.
categories.requires: an odds hand uses only 1s, 3s, 5s, 7s and 9s for its numbers, so look for it when odd numbers fill the rack

categories.howToSpot: Built mostly from N, E, W, S and the dragons, sometimes with a few numbers. Spot it when winds keep piling up on your rack.
categories.requires: this section is built mostly from winds and dragons, so a rack full of number tiles is not it

categories.howToSpot: Only 3s, 6s and 9s. It is a small, focused family, so if you hold several of those three numbers, look here.
categories.requires: 369 uses only 3s, 6s and 9s for its numbers, and it needs the 6 to tell it apart from a pure evens or pure odds hand

categories.howToSpot: No pungs or kongs, just single tiles and pairs. No jokers are allowed.
categories.requires: singles and pairs means no pungs or kongs at all, and no jokers anywhere

glossary.definition: One of the three number suits, marked with Chinese characters and usually printed in red. Nine numbers, four of each, and the Red Dragon is the crak family's dragon.
The bamboo suit, drawn as sticks. The 1 Bam is usually a bird rather than a single stick. The Green Dragon is the bam family's dragon.
The circle suit, drawn as rings of dots. The White Dragon, called the soap, is the dot family's dragon.
The White Dragon, so called because the plain-faced version looks like a bar of soap. It is the dot suit's dragon, and it also stands in for a zero in year hands.
The dragon paired with the crak suit. Any hand asking for a suit plus its dragon wants Red with craks.
The dragon paired with the bam suit. Any hand asking for a suit plus its dragon wants Green with bams.
North, East, West and South, four of each. They are honors, not numbers, so they never belong to a suit and never join a numeric run.
Eight flower tiles come in the set, and for card purposes any flower can stand in for any other. They are never part of a numbered run. Wherever the card shows an F, any flower works.

Eight wild tiles. A joker can stand in for a tile inside a group of three or more (a pung, kong or quint). It can never be a pair, a single, or part of a Singles and Pairs hand, and it can never be passed in the Charleston.
The winds and dragons together. They carry no number, so a rack full of honors points to the Winds and Dragons section.

An American set has 152 tiles. That is 108 numbers (three suits, nine numbers, four each), 16 winds, 12 dragons, 8 flowers and 8 jokers. Knowing that four of each tile exist is the basis of counting what is still live.
Two identical tiles. A pair can never be completed by calling a discard, except as the winning tile, and it can never contain a joker.
Three identical tiles. This is the smallest group you may call a discard for, and calling it means exposing the whole group on your rack.
Four identical tiles. Jokers are allowed inside one, so a kong can be part natural tiles and part jokers.
Five identical tiles, which is impossible without jokers because only four of any tile exist. Never plan a quint hand unless you are already holding jokers.
One lone tile the hand actually requires. Like a pair, it cannot hold a joker and cannot be called for, except as the tile that finishes your hand.
A called group laid face up on top of your rack for everyone to see. It tells the table which hands you can still make, and it shows you what other players are building.
A hand the card requires you to complete without exposing anything. You may still pick up the winning tile from a discard, but you may not call to expose a group along the way.
One family of hands on the card, such as the evens family or the consecutive runs. Reading which section a rack is chasing is the core skill this app drills.
One hand printed on the card, read left to right. Each section holds several lines, and the value beside each line says what it pays and whether it is X (exposures allowed) or C (concealed).

The tile-passing ritual before play begins. The first Charleston is required and goes right, then across, then left. A second Charleston, left then across then right, happens only if every player agrees to it.

The opening pass of three tiles to the player on your right. Like every pass except the last one of each Charleston, it must come from tiles you have looked at, so it is a good moment to pass your most isolated tiles.

Passing along tiles you have not looked at, taken straight from the set you were just handed. It is allowed only on the last pass of each Charleston (the first Left and the second Right), and it is useful when you have nothing to spare.
The last exchange, across the table only, of anywhere from zero to three tiles by mutual agreement. Both players have to pass the same number, so ask before you count on it.

Another name for the blind pass, meaning sending on some or all of the tiles you were just handed without looking at them. Allowed only on the last pass of each Charleston (the first Left and the second Right).
A joker may not leave your rack in any Charleston pass, blind or otherwise, or in the courtesy pass.

Claiming the tile just discarded to complete a pung, kong or quint that you then expose, or to win. You can call until the next player racks the tile they drew (or discards, or starts a joker swap). You cannot call a discard for a pair or a single unless it wins the hand for you.

A hand that can no longer legally win, usually because of an exposure that no card hand can match or a wrong mah jongg laid down. Once another player calls it dead and the tiles prove it, you stop drawing and discarding for the rest of the hand, but you still pay the winner. Nobody calls their own hand dead, so until someone does, keep playing and discard defensively.
Nobody declares mah jongg before the tiles run out. Until it ends, any opponent can still win and collect from you, so keep discarding carefully.

On your turn, after you draw or call and before you discard, trade a natural tile from your rack for a joker in any exposed group, your own included. The tile must be exactly the one the joker stands for, and the joker becomes yours to use. You may swap more than one in a turn.
A tile that plainly helps somebody at the table, usually because their exposures point at it. Late in a hand, throwing a hot tile can hand someone the win.

A tile no live hand seems to want, such as one already discarded twice with no reaction or one that clashes with every exposure on the table. Keeping one in reserve for the endgame is a habit worth building.
The call you make when your fourteenth tile completes a hand on the card. Say it before you expose your rack, and be sure, because laying down a wrong hand kills it.
The stand holding your tiles. Your concealed tiles rest on the sloped front; exposures sit on top of the rack where everyone can see them. Racked means in your hand, exposed means on top of the rack.
The face-down tiles everyone draws from. As it shrinks, the odds of anybody finishing shrink with it, which is when defense starts to matter more than your own hand.
The dealer's seat. East deals, starts with an extra tile, and throws the first discard. The seat rotates after each hand.

primer.body: Every player races to build a 14-tile hand that exactly matches one of the hands printed on the yearly card. Thirteen tiles live on your rack; the fourteenth is the tile you draw or call that completes the pattern. Complete it first and you call mahj.
primer.tip: Three of a kind is a pung. Most hands are built from groups like this.
primer.title: The goal

primer.body: Three suits run 1 through 9. They are craks (red), bams (green) and dots (blue). Winds are printed N, E, W, S. Each dragon goes with a suit, red with craks, green with bams and the blank soap with dots. Flowers are all interchangeable and show up in many card hands, and jokers stand in for tiles inside bigger groups.
primer.title: Meet the tiles

primer.body: The card groups its hands into sections, like even numbers or runs. You never memorize every hand. You learn to spot which section your rack is drifting toward, pick a target, and chase it. Keep a current card beside you to follow the lines.
primer.tip: All even numbers? Check the 2468 section first.
primer.title: Read the card

primer.body: Before play begins, everyone passes three unwanted tiles to the right, then across, then to the left, with an optional second round. Jokers never pass. The Charleston is how a messy deal becomes a plan.
primer.tip: Pass tiles that fit no section you are chasing. Never pass a joker.
primer.title: The Charleston

primer.body: On your turn, draw a tile, then discard one face up, either the tile you drew or one from your rack. You may also claim another player's discard to finish a group of 3, 4 or 5 matching tiles (a pung, kong or quint), then lay that group face up on your rack, which is called exposing it. Pairs and single tiles can only be claimed to finish your winning hand, and a hand marked C (concealed) on the card cannot expose anything before it wins. Match your whole hand to the card and you win.
primer.tip: A joker can sit inside a pung or bigger group, never in a pair or as a single tile.
primer.title: Play a turn

primer.body: That's the whole shape of the game. Build toward the card, survive the Charleston, and read racks fast. The drills teach each skill one room at a time, five minutes at a stretch.
primer.title: You're ready to train

referenceSections.watchOut: Soaps do double duty as zeros, so they get scarce fast. If two are already showing on other racks, the year hand you are chasing may already be out of reach.
Every odd tile you pick up is dead weight. If half your rack is odd after the Charleston, you are in the wrong section.
You need the same number across different suits, and only four of each exist. Losing one suit usually means losing the hand, so count what has been discarded before you commit.
Five of a kind, when only four of any tile exist. A quint hand is really a joker-count question. Without jokers in hand it is a hope, not a plan.
A flexible section, because the run can slide up or down a number while you wait, unless a line's note names its numbers. That flexibility is also a trap, since if you keep sliding you never commit.
The mirror of the evens family, with five numbers to build from instead of four.
Only sixteen winds and twelve dragons exist in the whole set, so honors dry up quickly. If nobody is discarding them, somebody else is collecting them too.
A narrow family built on three numbers across three suits. It reads clearly, so you know early whether you are in it. The downside is that there is nowhere to slide.
No jokers, anywhere. Because nothing can be called except the winning tile, you should not start one unless the tiles are already falling your way.

items.backBody: 36 tiles, numbered 1 through 9, four of each. On real tiles the number sits above a red Chinese character. Craks partner with the Red Dragon on the card.
36 tiles, numbered 1 through 9, four of each, drawn as green bamboo sticks. Bams partner with the Green Dragon. The 1 Bam is usually drawn as a bird, not a stick.
36 tiles, numbered 1 through 9, four of each, drawn as circles. Dots partner with the Soap (White Dragon).
16 tiles, four each of North, East, West and South. Winds & Dragons is the section built around them. A lone wind with no partner is a common early pass unless a line on your card wants it.

12 tiles, four each of Red, Green and Soap. Each dragon belongs to a suit. Red goes with Craks, Green with Bams, Soap with Dots. On the card, a dragon printed in the same color as a number group is that suit's own dragon. A different color means another suit's dragon.
The Soap is the White Dragon (it looks like a bar of soap). Besides being Dots' dragon, it stands in for zero in year hands, like the 0 in 2026.
8 flower tiles, and in American mahj they are all interchangeable. Any flower works wherever the card shows an F. Many card hands use flowers, so hold them early.

8 jokers. A joker stands in for any tile in a group of 3 or more (pung, kong, quint). It cannot be used in a pair or as a single tile, so Singles & Pairs hands never take one, and a joker can never be passed in the Charleston.
108 number tiles (three suits, 1-9, four each) + 16 winds + 12 dragons + 8 flowers + 8 jokers = 152. That is 8 more than the usual 144-tile Chinese set, and those 8 are the jokers.

The National Mah Jongg League (NMJL) card lists every legal winning hand this year, grouped in sections (2468, Consecutive Run, 13579...). A new card comes out every spring. Different colors on the card mean different suits, not particular ones. Any suit can be red, green or blue.
Pair = 2 identical tiles. Pung = 3. Kong = 4. Quint = 5 (only possible with jokers, since only four of each tile exist). Card hands are built from these blocks plus singles.

X = you may call discards and expose groups on your rack. C = concealed, so no exposures are allowed before mah jongg (you may still call the final winning tile). Check the value printed beside each line to see what it pays.

items.frontTitle: C vs X on the Card

items.explanation: Red goes with Craks. Remember C for Crak, R for Red. Green belongs to Bams, Soap to Dots.
items.prompt: Which dragon goes with a crak hand?

items.explanation: Green goes with Bams, because bamboo is green.
items.prompt: Which dragon belongs to the bam suit?

items.explanation: Soap (the White Dragon) goes with Dots. Red goes with Craks and Green with Bams.
items.prompt: Which dragon matches a dot hand?

items.explanation: Never. Jokers only work in groups of 3 or more (pung, kong, quint). Pairs and singles must be the real tiles.
items.prompt: Can a joker complete a pair?

items.explanation: Jokers may never be passed in the Charleston or the courtesy pass. Passing one breaks the rules.
items.prompt: Can you pass a joker in the Charleston?

items.explanation: The Soap (White Dragon) doubles as zero. 2026 = 2, Soap, 2, 6.
items.prompt: In a year hand like 2026, what stands in for the 0?

items.explanation: Eight jokers, and counting them helps. If you've seen 6 on racks and discards, only 2 are left in play.
items.prompt: How many jokers are in an American mahj set?

items.explanation: Three identical tiles. Unlike other mahjong styles, you can't claim a discard for a run like 5-6-7. The card spells out every shape.
items.prompt: What is a pung?

items.explanation: Jokers. Only four of each tile exist, so every quint needs at least one.
items.prompt: Only four of each tile exist. How is a quint (5 of a kind) possible?

choices: Yes, any flower is any F
items.explanation: In American mahj every flower is identical for play. If the card says FF, any two flowers work.
items.prompt: Are all 8 flowers interchangeable?

items.explanation: Never. Singles & Pairs hands have no groups of 3 or more, and jokers only work in groups of 3 or more.
items.prompt: Jokers in a Singles & Pairs hand?

items.explanation: Concealed. You can't call discards to expose groups, so the hand stays on your rack until you call the winning tile for mah jongg.
items.prompt: Each hand on the card is marked X or C. What does C mean?

items.explanation: Different colors mean different suits, not particular ones. Green, red and blue just tell you the hand uses three suits, and you pick which is which.
items.prompt: A card hand shows numbers in green, red, and blue. What do the colors mean?

items.explanation: Thirteen. You draw a 14th, then discard (or keep it and discard something else). East is the one exception, starting the game with 14 and opening by discarding. Mah jongg is 14 tiles matching a card hand exactly.
items.prompt: How many tiles do you hold during play (before your turn)?

items.explanation: Yes. On your turn, before you discard, you may give the real matching tile to any exposure holding a joker, yours or an opponent's, and take the joker into your hand. Check every exposure for jokers you can take.
items.prompt: An opponent's exposed kong contains a joker. You hold the real matching tile. Can you swap?

items.explanation: A discarded joker is dead, so nobody can call it for anything. It is safe to throw, but you give up your most flexible tile, which is why it is rarely worth it.
items.prompt: Someone discards a joker. Can you call it?

drills.subtitle: Quick quiz: dragons, jokers, and the basic tile rules
drills.title: Tile Check

items.explanation: 152: the 144 base tiles (suits, winds, dragons, flowers) plus the 8 jokers that make American mahj its own game.
items.prompt: How many tiles are in a standard American Mah Jongg set?

items.explanation: Green goes with Bams. Red goes with Craks, Soap goes with Dots. When a hand wants a dragon in a suit, the card means THAT suit's dragon.
items.prompt: The Green Dragon belongs with which suit?

choices: Any four tiles in a row
items.explanation: Four identical tiles. Pung is 3, kong is 4, quint is 5 (and a quint always needs a joker, since only 4 of each tile exist).
items.prompt: What is a kong?

choices: They stay hidden on your rack
They go face up on top of your rack for the rest of the hand
You show them once, then hide them
You hand them to the discarder
items.explanation: They stay face up on your rack for good. That is why calling is a commitment: everyone can see your section, and you cannot switch to a concealed hand afterward.
items.prompt: You call a discard to complete a pung. What happens to those tiles?

choices: The player closest to the discarder's right
items.explanation: Mah jongg always wins the tile. A winning hand outranks any exposure call, no matter who called first or where they sit.
items.prompt: One player calls a discard for a pung, another calls the same tile for mah jongg. Who gets it?

items.explanation: Four of each wind, the same as every other tile. That is worth knowing: if three Easts are already visible, the fourth is the last one alive.
items.prompt: How many East wind tiles are in the set?

choices: Yes, any tile you need can be called
No, unless that tile completes your mah jongg
Only if you expose the pair
items.explanation: Discards can only be called to make a group of 3 or more, or to win. A pair is not an exposure, so the only way to claim a discard for a pair is if it is your winning tile.
items.prompt: You need one tile to complete a PAIR and it gets discarded. Can you call it?

choices: Nothing, you just take it back
Anyone can call your hand dead, and then you stop playing
You swap it for a joker
items.explanation: Every exposure has to belong to a real hand on the card. Once another player calls your hand dead and the exposure proves it, you stop drawing and discarding for the rest of the hand, and you still pay the winner. Check the card before you call.
items.prompt: You expose a pung that fits no hand on the card. What happens?

choices: No, only pungs can be called
Only with a joker in it
items.explanation: You can call a discard for a pung, a kong or a quint, as long as you expose the whole group. Pairs and singles are the ones you can only call to win.
items.prompt: A discard would finish a kong for you. Can you call it?

items.explanation: Four real tiles is the most you can have, so the other two of the six have to be jokers.
items.prompt: Only four of each tile exist. What does a sextet (six of a kind) need?

items.explanation: Eight flowers, and unlike suited tiles they are all interchangeable with each other.
items.prompt: How many flower tiles are in an American mah jongg set?

items.explanation: Twelve: four Red, four Green and four Soap. Sixteen is the winds. With only four of each dragon, a dragon kong takes every copy or a joker.
items.prompt: How many dragon tiles are in an American set?

items.explanation: A bird, often a peacock or sparrow. It is still just the 1 Bam: a bam tile, and one of the four copies.
items.prompt: Many sets draw the 1 Bam as something other than a single stick. What is it usually?

choices: When the exposure is yours only
On your turn, for any exposed joker whose tile you hold
items.explanation: On your turn you may redeem any exposed joker, including an opponent's, by giving the real tile it stands for.
items.prompt: When may you swap a real tile for a joker in an exposure?

items.explanation: Thirteen tiles, except East who starts with fourteen and discards first.
items.prompt: How many tiles does a player hold after the deal, before the first discard?

items.explanation: The white dragon, or soap, stands in for the zero in a year. It is still a dragon everywhere else on the card.
items.prompt: In Year hands, what does the soap usually represent?

items.backBody: Built around the current year's digits, with soaps standing in for zeros. Spot it when you're holding 2s and soaps. The digits are easy to spot on a rack, but year lines are specific, so read them closely.
Only even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8). Every odd tile in your hand is dead weight for this section. If your deal is heavy on 2s, 4s, 6s and 8s, start here and pass every odd tile.
The same number collected across different suits. Spot it when one number keeps showing up in two or three suits at once. A good fallback when one number keeps turning up in several suits.

Needs five of a kind, and only four of each tile exist, so quints are impossible without jokers. Only chase these when you're joker-rich. As a rule of thumb, don't commit to Quints with fewer than two jokers.

Numbers that step up in order, like 4-5-6-7. Unless a line's note names its numbers, a run can start on any number, so a deal with numbers in a row can fit more than one line. Read the note beside each line, because a run that names its numbers cannot slide.

Only odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7, 9). The mirror image of 2468, with one more number to build from. Count how many lines your card gives this section. The more lines it has, the more places an odd-heavy deal can go.

Built mostly from N, E, W, S and the dragons, sometimes with a few numbers. Spot it when winds keep piling up on your rack. Count the winds on your rack. With one or two, plan to pass them. With four or five, consider committing here.
Only 3s, 6s and 9s. It is a small, focused family, so if you hold several of those three numbers, look here. The 3s and 9s are odd and the 6s are even, so a 369 start can still move to 13579 or 2468.

No pungs or kongs, just single tiles and pairs. No jokers are allowed. Because nothing can be called except the winning tile, every other tile must be drawn or come through the Charleston. That makes it a hard target for a new player.
A dragon printed in the same color as a number group is that suit's own dragon. 4 Craks go with the Red Dragon, so this fits. Green would belong with bams, and Soap with dots.
items.backTitle: Yes, Same Color Means Same Suit
items.frontSubtitle: Do your tiles fill that part of the line?
items.frontTitle: A line shows 4444 and a D, both in the same color.

items.backBody: A dragon in a different color from the numbers has to come from a different suit. Green is the bams' own dragon, so it matches these 4 Bams instead of contrasting with them. A Red Dragon or a Soap would fit.
items.backTitle: No, Different Color Means Different Suit
items.frontSubtitle: Do your tiles fill that part of the line?
items.frontTitle: A line shows 4444 in one color and a D in a different color.

items.backBody: In Any Like Numbers the 1s are a placeholder. Any number works as long as every group on the line uses the same one, so 7s in the colors the line shows are just as good as 1s.
items.frontSubtitle: Can you play it with 7s instead?
items.frontTitle: A Like Numbers line is printed with 1s.

items.backBody: Run lines show the lowest numbers. Unless the note beside the line names its numbers, you can start higher, as long as the numbers stay in order with no gaps.
items.backTitle: Yes, Unless the Line Says Otherwise
items.frontSubtitle: Can you play it with 5s, 6s and 7s?
items.frontTitle: A Consecutive Run line is printed with 1s, 2s and 3s.

items.backBody: C means concealed, so nothing may be exposed before mah jongg. Once a group is face up on your rack, every C line is closed to you and only X lines can still win.
items.frontSubtitle: Can you still win with that line?
items.frontTitle: Your target line is marked C, and you already exposed a pung.

items.backBody: NEWS means one North, one East, one West and one South, four single tiles. Jokers never fill a single, so every wind has to be the real tile.
items.frontSubtitle: Can the joker stand in for the West?

items.backBody: Used as a zero, the Soap goes with any suit. It only has to line up with Dots when it is playing its other role, as the dots' dragon.
items.backTitle: Yes, a Zero Has No Suit
items.frontTitle: Your year hand's 2s and 6 are Craks.

drills.subtitle: Flashcards: every card section, and how to read a line
drills.title: Know the Sections

items.explanation: Every number tile is even, from 2s to 8s across the suits. The flowers and the joker point nowhere else, so the numbers decide and the read is 2468.
The rack holds 3-4-5, 4-5-6 and 5-6-7, stepping numbers in all three suits. Mixed odds and evens rule out 2468 and 13579, so Consecutive Run is the read.
Every number is odd except one stray 2 Dot. Three pairs of odd bams is a solid 13579 start. The 2 Dot and the lone wind are your first passes.
Eight winds including a pung of Norths, plus two dragons, and only one number tile in the whole rack. The read is Winds & Dragons.
Every number is a 3, 6 or 9 except the stray 2 Bam. A pung of 6 Craks plus pairs of 9s gives the 369 section a solid start.
Eight fives across all three suits. When one number fills your rack like this, Any Like Numbers is the read.
The 2s, soaps (zeros) and 6s are the makings of a year hand. 2468 fits too, but the soaps point to the year section first.
Two pungs of 7s and three jokers. Two jokers turn one pung into a quint, and the third turns the other pung into a kong. Only jokers can make a quint, so a joker-rich rack points at Quints.
Six natural pairs and no jokers, mixing odd and even numbers. Pairs in Singles & Pairs must be natural because jokers can't fill them, so a rack that already holds this many pairs is a strong start.

drills.subtitle: See 13 tiles, name the section they're chasing
drills.title: Read the Rack

items.explanation: Every number tile is odd: 1s, 3s, 5s, 7s, 9s, with a pung of 3 Craks in hand. The flowers and the joker do not point anywhere else, so the numbers decide: this is a 13579 rack.
4-5-6, 5-6-7, 6-7-8: three stepped runs, one per suit. The mix of odds and evens kills both 13579 and 2468, and the 4s, 5s, 7s and 8s kill 369.
Eight winds, a pung of Easts, and three dragons, with not one number tile on the rack. Any section built on numbers would be starting from nothing. Winds and Dragons it is.

The soaps are the tell. Soap stands in for zero, so 2s, Soaps, and 6s spell out the year, and year hands often use flowers. 2468 is the decoy, but with no 4s and no 8s anywhere it never really had a shot.
Two pungs of 3s and FOUR jokers. Only jokers can make a quint, and these four can stretch either pung into a quint, or both. Joker-rich racks with big groups point at Quints.

Six natural pairs and zero jokers, odd and even mixed. A rack that is already all pairs is a good start for Singles and Pairs, and every pair in that section must be natural, since it never takes jokers.
Every number on this rack is even, with not an odd tile in sight, so 2468 is the read.
Three, four, five, six: the numbers step up in order. A run always mixes odd and even, so it can never be an evens or odds hand.
Not one numbered tile on the rack. When honors pile up like this, Winds and Dragons is the clear read: any section built on numbers would be starting from nothing.
Only 3s, 6s and 9s. The 6 rules out a pure odds hand and the 3 and 9 rule out a pure evens hand, so 369 is the read.
The same number in all three suits is the signature of Any Like Numbers. One number arriving from every direction is the cue to look here.

items.backBody: Before play starts, everyone passes tiles. That is three passes (right, across, left), an optional second round (left, across, right), then an optional courtesy pass across. Each Charleston pass is 3 tiles. The point is to trade tiles you don't need for ones you might.
items.frontSubtitle: How the passing before play works

items.backBody: Rack your tiles by suit and number, then shortlist 2-3 card sections your deal leans toward. Don't commit to one hand yet. Pass the tiles that help none of your shortlist.
items.frontSubtitle: What do you do with a fresh deal?

items.backBody: Jokers may never be passed in the Charleston or courtesy pass. If you're ever handed one, someone broke the rules. Flowers can be passed, but early on it is better to keep them.
Many card hands use flowers, so a flower is rarely a dead tile early on. Keep them in the early passes. Once you are committed to a hand with no F in it, they become passes.
Jokers can't fill a pair, so natural pairs anchor a hand. Pass lone strays (single winds, isolated numbers) before you split a pair, unless the pair fits none of the sections you are considering.
items.frontSubtitle: You must pass three tiles. Which ones?

items.backBody: On the last pass of each Charleston (the first Left and the second Right), you may pass on 1 to 3 of the tiles just handed to you without looking at them. You still pass three tiles, but each blind one lets you keep one of your own. Use it when you don't want to give up tiles you need.

The second Charleston only happens if all players agree, so any one player can stop it. If your hand is already strong after round one, say stop. Another round means more tiles leaving your rack, which a strong hand may not need.
After the Charleston, you and the player across can swap 0 to 3 tiles. You each pass the same number, agreed out loud ('two?'). Ask for fewer if your hand is close.

Tiles that arrive are often ones the passer didn't need, unless they were passed blind. Three winds from your right? That player probably isn't on Winds & Dragons. Treat it as a hint, not proof, since blind passes tell you nothing.

When your strays are equally useless to you, mix them across your passes rather than sending three of one family (say, 2C 4C 6C) to one player. The edge is small, so never keep a tile you need just to split a bundle.

items.backBody: It's an odd number in a suit you're not using, so it misses your hand twice. The only reason to hold a tile like this is defense late in the game. Early on, it's your cleanest discard.
items.frontSubtitle: You draw 3 Bam. Keep or throw?
items.frontTitle: You're building 2468 in craks and dots.

items.backBody: While your hand could still change, a spare flower is insurance. You can swap it for a joker in someone's flower exposure, and switching lines can change how many flowers you need. Once you are locked into a line with exactly two, it becomes a fine discard.
items.frontSubtitle: You draw a third F. Keep or throw?
items.frontTitle: You hold FF and your hand needs exactly two flowers.

items.backBody: Rebuild the hand around the joker. A joker can rescue any section except Singles & Pairs. Re-scan the card for sections where your joker plus your longest tiles fit. Only late in the hand, with no way left to win, is a joker the safest discard you own, because nobody can call it.
items.frontSubtitle: Bail on the hand or the joker?
items.frontTitle: Your hand is going nowhere, but you hold a joker.

items.backBody: On your turn, place your real 6 Bam on their exposure and take the joker. You trade one tile for a more flexible one, so check the exposures on the table for jokers every turn.
items.frontSubtitle: You just drew the real 6 Bam. Now what?
items.frontTitle: An opponent's exposed kong shows a joker.

items.backBody: Jokers can't be used in Singles & Pairs, which has no groups of 3 or more. If you're truly close, play on. If you're 4 or more tiles away, this joker is a good reason to switch sections.
items.frontSubtitle: You draw a joker. Good news?

items.backBody: Only four copies of every tile. If one 5 Crak is in the discards and one is exposed, your pair of 5 Craks can never become a pung without a joker. Counting visible copies tells you when a hand can no longer be made.
items.frontTitle: How many 5 Craks exist in the whole set?

items.backBody: An exposure narrows their hand to the card lines that use it. An evens hand, a run through 4, or a like-numbers hand of 4s could all fit. Before discarding another 4, or an even number such as 2, 6 or 8, pause and think about what their exposure could belong to.
items.frontTitle: Your left opponent exposes a pung of 4 Dots.

items.backBody: Follow the count. The hand with more tiles home needs fewer lucky draws, unless the other is far more flexible or pays far more. Recount every few draws, because the best hand for your rack changes as tiles arrive.
items.frontTitle: Two tiles fit Hand A. Nine tiles fit Hand B.

items.backBody: A natural pung of winds is a real asset, but only in a hand that calls for one. Check your card for lines that use it. Keep it if you can commit to one of them. If your hand lives elsewhere, a wind pung is three dead tiles.
items.backTitle: Keep It If a Line Uses It
items.frontTitle: Early in the hand, you hold N N and draw a third North.

items.backBody: All eight flowers are interchangeable, so any flower you throw fits anyone collecting flowers. An East fits only a player collecting Easts, and only three others exist. Neither is truly safe, but early on the lone wind is usually the lighter throw.
items.frontTitle: Early in the game, you must throw a flower or a lone wind.

items.backBody: A discarded joker cannot be called, so it is safe, but it is gone for good. Three jokers can rescue a slow hand. They can fill pungs of anything you hold two of, kongs, even quints. Look for a new line before you give one up.
items.frontTitle: Your hand looks hopeless and you hold three jokers.

items.backBody: Calling locks you onto hands that fit the exposure, tells the table your section, and kills any concealed hand. Call when it moves a hand you are already committed to clearly closer to done, not just because you can.
items.frontTitle: You can call that discard for an exposed pung.

items.backBody: Concealed only bans exposures before the win. Any hand, concealed or not, may call the final winning tile. If the tile wins your hand, call it.
items.frontTitle: Your hand is concealed (marked C) and someone throws your winning tile.

items.backBody: Prefer tiles matching no exposure on their rack, tiles others already threw without anyone calling them, and tiles with 3 copies already visible. Those are safer, not safe. Jokers can still finish a group, and a lone tile can be their winner. Sometimes the right play is breaking your own hand to avoid throwing it.
items.frontSubtitle: How do you pick a discard?
items.frontTitle: It's late, one opponent is clearly close.

drills.subtitle: Make the call, then flip to see the coach's answer
drills.title: Keep or Throw

choices: Only to complete an exposure you can show, or to declare mah jongg
items.explanation: You call a discard to complete a pung, kong or quint that you then expose, or to finish your hand. You cannot call for a pair or a single unless it is your winning tile.
items.prompt: Another player discards a tile you need. When may you call it?

choices: An exposure that cannot belong to any hand on the card
items.explanation: If your exposures do not match any hand on the card, the hand is dead. Check the card before you expose, not after.
items.prompt: Which of these makes a hand dead?

choices: A tile you have not seen anyone discard
A tile of a kind already discarded twice with no takers
A tile that fits the pattern of an opponent's exposures
items.explanation: A tile discarded twice without being called is the safest of these, since the table has already shown it does not want it. Safer is not safe, because it can still be someone's last tile, but it beats a tile that fits their exposures or giving up a flower.
items.prompt: Late in the hand, which discard is usually safest?

items.explanation: Two even pungs point toward 2468. An odds hand cannot use them, a 369 hand cannot use the 4s, and Singles and Pairs never uses a pung. Stop feeding them even tiles and watch which numbers they still need.
items.prompt: An opponent exposes a pung of 4 Bams and a pung of 6 Dots. Which of these sections do they most likely point toward?

items.explanation: Singles and Pairs contains no pungs or kongs, so there is nothing to call and nothing to expose. It is played entirely from your own rack.
items.prompt: Which section's hands can never be exposed?

choices: The discarder pays double, the other two pay the hand's value
items.explanation: Throwing the winning tile costs double. The other two players pay the value printed beside the hand on the card.
items.prompt: You win on another player's discard. Who pays what?

choices: All three pay the hand's value
items.explanation: Nobody fed you the winning tile, so everyone pays double.
items.prompt: You win on a tile you drew from the wall yourself. Who pays?

items.explanation: A jokerless win pays double. Singles and Pairs hands are the exception, because they can never hold a joker, so they earn no bonus for going without.
items.prompt: You win with a hand outside Singles and Pairs, and it has no jokers. What changes?

choices: Nothing extra, bonuses do not combine
items.explanation: Both bonuses apply. Drawing it yourself doubles the payment, and jokerless doubles it again, so each player pays four times the hand's value. Singles and Pairs earn no jokerless bonus, so the same win there pays double.
items.prompt: You draw your own winning tile. The hand has no jokers and is not a Singles and Pairs hand. What does each player pay?

items.explanation: A wall game costs nothing. The tiles are reshuffled and the next hand is dealt.
items.prompt: The wall runs out and nobody has won. Who pays?

choices: No, a dead hand is out of the game
items.explanation: A dead hand cannot win and stops drawing and discarding, but you are still at the table, so you pay the winner like everyone else.
items.prompt: Your hand went dead earlier, and another player wins. Do you pay?

choices: Once the next player has drawn from the wall and racked the tile
As soon as the tile touches the table
Only after the next discard lands
Never, discards stay callable all game
items.explanation: You may call until the next player has drawn a tile and put it on their rack. After that, the discard is gone. Speak up quickly.
items.prompt: When is it too late to call a discard?

choices: Draw from the wall, then discard
Expose the pung and draw a replacement tile
items.explanation: Calling takes the place of your draw. Put the pung face up on your rack, discard, and play continues to your right.
items.prompt: You call a discard for a pung. What comes next?

choices: The player whose turn comes next
items.explanation: When two players want a tile for an exposure, it goes to the one next in turn after the discarder, unless the other caller has already put the tile on their rack or exposed tiles for it. A call for mah jongg still beats any exposure.
items.prompt: Two players call the same discard for a pung. Who gets it?

choices: No, it locked when you discarded
Only if it wins the hand
items.explanation: Once you have discarded after exposing it, a group is locked. The fourth 5 Bam stays on your rack or goes to the discards. The one change still allowed is someone swapping a real tile for a joker in it.
items.prompt: You have an exposed pung of 5 Bams and draw the fourth. Can you add it to make a kong?

choices: Pick the tiles back up and keep playing
Your hand is dead, and the other three play on
items.explanation: Once a wrong hand is laid down, it is dead. The other three keep playing, and you still pay whoever wins. Check the card before you lay down.
items.prompt: You call mah jongg, lay your hand down, and it turns out one tile is wrong. What happens?

drills.subtitle: Calling, exposures, scoring, dead hands, and safe discards
drills.title: Table Rules

items.backBody: Once its owner has discarded, an exposed pung can never grow into a kong, so they cannot use it there. With three exposed and one in your hand, all four 6 Dots are accounted for, so nobody can hold a natural pair of them. Only a player waiting on it as a single, or one ready to back it with jokers, could still want one. It is one of the safer discards you have.
items.frontSubtitle: You just drew the fourth 6 Dot, and your hand does not need it. Keep or throw?
items.frontTitle: An opponent has an exposed PUNG of three natural 6 Dots.

items.backBody: A lone North with no partner needs two more Norths or jokers just to make a pung, and your hand is not built on winds. Early, before anyone commits, it is close to a free discard. The same tile late, after someone exposes winds, is a live grenade.
items.frontSubtitle: Your hand is built on numbers, and nobody has exposed a wind. Keep or throw?
items.frontTitle: Turn 3. You hold one North and no other winds.

items.backBody: Straddling two sections means every draw helps only half your hand and you never get close to either. Count the tiles you still need, commit to the smaller number, and turn the other section's tiles into discards.
items.frontTitle: You are 3 tiles from a 2468 hand and 4 from a Consecutive Run.

items.backBody: A tile the table has already passed on twice is safer than the flower, though not safe: it can still be someone's last tile, and jokers can still finish a group. Flowers are the opposite: many hands use them, so a late flower can easily be the tile someone is waiting for.
items.frontTitle: Late game. You must discard: a spare flower, or a wind already thrown twice?

items.backBody: Calling exposes the group for good and locks you out of every concealed hand on the card. Trading a hand you are 2 tiles from for a hand you are half on is a bad trade, no matter how satisfying the call feels.
items.frontSubtitle: Your other option: a concealed hand you are 2 tiles from. Call it?
items.frontTitle: Turn 4. Calling this discard gives you a pung for a hand you are only half on.

items.backBody: Only four of any tile exist. Yours plus the three gone makes four, so there are no 5 Bams left to draw and your pung would need two jokers. Count the dead tiles before you count on a group: the discard pile tells you which hands are already over.

options: Switch to a hand that does not need 5 Bams

items.frontSubtitle: You hold one. Two are in the discards, one is exposed on a rack. Keep chasing?
items.frontTitle: You need a pung of 5 Bams.

items.backBody: You can redeem a joker from your own exposure, not just an opponent's. The 8 Crak goes on the pung, the joker comes back to your rack, and now it can fill a group you still need.
items.frontSubtitle: You draw the real 8 Crak. Swap it in?
items.frontTitle: Your own exposed pung of 8 Craks holds a joker.

items.backBody: Singles and pairs can't be called for an exposure, but any tile can be called when it wins the hand. Call it, then lay down your hand.
items.frontSubtitle: Someone discards a 5 Dot. Can you call it?
items.frontTitle: You are one tile from mah jongg: a lone 5 Dot.

items.backBody: A single honor that belongs to no section you are chasing is pure dead weight. The earlier it goes, the safer it is.
items.frontSubtitle: Your hand is going 2468. Keep or throw?

items.backBody: All four are accounted for, so no real 5 Crak can still reach you. Waiting on one is waiting on nothing. The pair is still a pair, but it can only become a pung with a joker, so do not count on a third copy. Count before you commit.
items.frontSubtitle: The other two are already exposed elsewhere. Keep waiting for a third?

items.backBody: Jokers can never be passed, in the Charleston or the courtesy pass. Even if they could, they are the most valuable tiles on your rack.
items.frontSubtitle: Pass a joker to speed things up?

items.backBody: Flowers are useful in most sections, but a Singles and Pairs hand may only want a pair of them. Holding a third out of habit costs you a tile you need.
items.frontTitle: Three flowers, hand is Singles and Pairs

items.backBody: Switching late means starting over with fewer tiles left in the wall. Only jump when the new hand is genuinely closer than the one you are on.
items.frontTitle: Seven tiles from mah jongg, late in the wall

drills.subtitle: Thirteen more calls: safe discards, dead tiles, joker swaps, and when NOT to call
drills.title: Keep or Throw: Extra Reps

items.reasoning: Count both roads. The odds side has eight odd tiles with two pairs (1 and 9 Crak). The run side is only the 5-6-7 in Bams, three tiles, and your Craks (1, 3, 7, 9) have gaps, so they add little to it. Commit to 13579. Keep 5 Bam and 7 Bam since they are odd, and pass the evens an odds hand can't use: 6 Bam, 2 Dot and 4 Dot.
items.situation: First Charleston, pass RIGHT. Your craks scream odds, your bams start a run. Pick 3.
items.tip: When two sections compete, follow the count. The longer, paired side wins; the shorter side becomes your passes.

items.reasoning: The three odd Dots (3, 5, 7) fit none of your even plan, so they are clean passes. Your 2468 lean is only six tiles so far, so the Reds stay as a backup. Do NOT break the Red pair when you have cleaner tiles to give. Jokers can never build a pair, so a natural pair is hard to rebuild once it is gone.
items.situation: First Charleston, pass RIGHT. You lean toward 2468, and you also hold a pair of Red Dragons. Pick 3.
items.tip: Hold natural pairs by default, and break one only when every other pass costs more.

items.reasoning: Usually you protect pairs, but a pair of Norths does not fit the evens you are collecting, and you already hold eight even tiles and a joker, so here the pair is the cheapest thing to give. Pass both Norths and the odd 5 Dot rather than give up an even tile or a flower.
items.situation: First Charleston, pass RIGHT. Eight even tiles plus a lonely pair of Norths. Pick 3.
items.tip: Hold pairs by default, but a pair that fits none of your target section is fair to pass early, before opponents lock in.

items.reasoning: 369 and a run overlap here. 369 uses ten of your twelve numbers, every 3, 6 and 9. A run on the 3-4-5-6 core uses eight, and it cannot reach your four 9s without 7s and 8s you do not hold. 369 is ahead, so commit to it, keep the 6 Dot and 9 Crak pairs, and pass the 4 Bam and 5 Bam, which 369 has no use for, with the lone North.
items.situation: First Charleston, pass ACROSS. Your hand reads as both 369 and Consecutive Run. Pick 3.
items.tip: When 369 and Run overlap, count how many of your tiles each one can use. Commit to whichever uses more.

items.reasoning: Seven 6s across three suits is a strong Like Numbers start, so this pass is a chance to clear out the tiles that do not serve it. The lone 9 Crak and 3 Dot do nothing for the 6s (at best a long-shot backup), and every other choice breaks up your 6s or gives up a flower, so they are the cheapest to give, with the North. Keep both flowers, since many hands use them. Remember that the second Charleston is optional: any one player can stop it.
items.situation: Second Charleston, pass LEFT. Nobody stopped the second Charleston, so it goes ahead. You hold seven 6s across three suits. Pick 3.
items.tip: Any player can stop the second Charleston, so know before it starts whether you still want three more passes.

items.reasoning: Your tiles cluster on 4s through 7s, the makings of a Consecutive Run with a 6 Dot pair, so the 2 Bam, 9 Dot and East are the strays. Your LAST pass is also defense: your right-hand neighbor passed you three winds, so they are probably not collecting winds, which makes the East a fairly safe tile to send them.
items.situation: Second Charleston, the last pass, going RIGHT. On an earlier left pass your right-hand neighbor handed you three winds, so they are probably not on Winds and Dragons. Pick 3.
items.tip: Your final pass is a defensive tool. Feed a neighbor the kind of tile they have hinted they do not want.

drills.subtitle: Torn deals, pair math, and defending with your pass
drills.title: Advanced Charleston

items.explanation: The same number in two suits is the Like Numbers tell, and kongs of it make the read even stronger. Whatever their exact hand, it is made of 6s: the 6 Dot is the tile to hold. Exposures cannot grow once play moves on, so read them as they sit.
items.prompt: An opponent exposes a kong of 6 Bams AND a kong of 6 Craks. Which discard is most dangerous?

items.explanation: A run through both 3 and 9 would have to cover seven numbers, so Consecutive Run is a long shot. Threes and nines together are a 369 tell (an odds hand can use them too). Treat 3s, 6s, and 9s as hot tiles against this player.
items.prompt: An opponent exposes a pung of 3 Dots and a pung of 9 Dots. Which of these sections fits?

items.explanation: Only four of any tile exist. You hold one and two are in the discards, so at most one is left, and it could be buried in the wall or stuck in a hand. Even if it comes, that is a pair: the pung needs a joker. Start lining up a backup.
items.prompt: You hold one North and want a pung. Two Norths already sit in the discards. How many more Norths can still reach you?

choices: Only if you draw two more jokers first
items.explanation: A quint needs five tiles, and only four 5 Dots exist. With three gone, you would have to build almost the whole group from jokers. That is a fantasy, not a plan. Count the naturals before you chase any quint, and fold this one.
items.prompt: You are chasing a quint (five of a kind) of 5 Dots using jokers. Three 5 Dots are already visible around the table. Keep pushing?

items.explanation: Their North pung locked when they discarded, so it can never become a kong, and with three Norths on their rack and one in yours, nobody else holds a natural North to build with. A middle number or a soap can still fit a winds and dragons hand, and flowers fit many hands.
items.prompt: One opponent has exposed a pung of North and a pung of Red, and has discarded since. You hold the fourth North. Which discard is safest against them?

items.explanation: Two pungs in one suit, two numbers apart, read as a run with the middle missing: the 7 Bam is the bridge that would complete it. Hold it and throw something unrelated.
items.prompt: An opponent has exposed a pung of 6 Bams and a pung of 8 Bams and is waiting for a tile. Which discard is most dangerous?

choices: Draw and hope your own hand comes together
Switch to defense: discard only tiles they cannot use, even if it breaks your hand
Discard fast to end the game sooner
items.explanation: If you cannot win, your job is to not deal the winning tile. Break your own hand and throw tiles their exposures prove are safe. A blocked win is a good outcome when yours is hopeless.
items.prompt: Your hand is hopeless, and an opponent is one tile away from mah jongg on an obvious hand. What is the right play?

choices: Call the joker off the discard pile
Swap your real 3 Crak for the joker and take the joker into your hand
items.explanation: This is the joker exchange. On your turn, before you discard, you may redeem an exposed joker by giving the matching natural tile, and the joker comes into your hand. A free joker is a huge tempo swing, so watch for these.
items.prompt: An opponent has an exposed pung of 3 Craks made with two real tiles and one joker. You hold a real 3 Crak. On your turn you may:

choices: Any player can redeem them with the matching tile, so plan to grab them
They score bonus points at the end
They stop you from using your own jokers
items.explanation: Exposed jokers are up for grabs. A single spare natural tile can pull one into your hand on your turn. Knowing which jokers are live tells you when a swap is waiting for you.
items.prompt: Why bother tracking the jokers sitting in opponents' exposures?

items.explanation: Everyone holds thirteen between turns. Nine are showing in the three pungs, so only four are hidden, and those four plus one more tile make the hand. The fewer tiles hidden, the easier they are to read and the closer they usually are.
items.prompt: Between turns, an opponent has three pungs face up. How many of their tiles are still hidden?

choices: About as safe as a throw gets
Illegal, the same tile cannot follow
Only safe if you are East
items.explanation: Every other player just had the chance to take that exact tile and passed. Following a fresh discard is a classic safe throw. It is not a guarantee: one draw can change a hand, so it is safest right away.
items.prompt: The player on your left just threw a 4 Bam and nobody called it. You hold a 4 Bam. How risky is throwing it now?

choices: Nothing is proven safe against them, they may be close on a concealed hand
They cannot win without calling a discard
items.explanation: No exposures means no information, not no danger. A concealed hand can be one tile away with nothing showing. Lean on tiles the table has already let pass.
items.prompt: Late in the hand, one opponent has exposed nothing and is discarding calmly. What does that tell you?

drills.subtitle: Read exposures, count tiles, and stop feeding winners
drills.title: Defense School

items.explanation: 369 is the decoy: there is a 6 in every suit and a 9 Bam. But the 4 and 5 Crak, the 7 and 8 Bam, and the 5 and 7 Dots are dead weight for 369, while they make 4-5-6, 6-7-8-9 and 5-6-7 runs, one in each suit. Stepping numbers like these make this Consecutive Run.
Consecutive Run is the decoy, tempted by the 3, 5 and 6 Bams. But ten of your eleven numbers are 3s, 6s and 9s, including three pairs, and the 5 Bam is the only number 369 cannot use. This is 369.
Year is the decoy because of the 2s, 6s, and flowers. But a year hand needs soaps as its zeros, and there are none. With 4s and 8s in the mix, tiles a year hand never uses, this is a straight 2468.
2468 is the decoy since 2s and 6s are even. But the soaps are the giveaway: they stand in for the zeros in 2, 0, 2, 6. With no 4s or 8s and a fistful of flowers, this is a Year hand.

Singles and Pairs is the decoy, since you have several pairs. But a Singles and Pairs hand has no pungs and no jokers, and this rack has a pung of 5 Bams and a joker, so it does not fit. Read it as 13579.
13579 is the decoy off the 1s, 3s, and 5s, but the 2, 6, and 8 pairs kill any odd-only hand. Six natural pairs across mixed numbers with zero jokers is the textbook Singles and Pairs shape.

Quints is the decoy, dreaming of five 7s in a suit. But your 7s sit in pungs and pairs, which need two or three jokers each to reach five, and you hold just one. Eight 7s spread across all three suits reads as Any Like Numbers instead.
Year is the decoy: the soaps and 2s hint at 2, 0, 2, 6. But there is not a single 6, and three dragon pairs plus three winds are already on the rack. That is Winds and Dragons.

drills.subtitle: Ambiguous racks where two sections look right
drills.title: Expert Rack Reading

items.explanation: Jokers never fill a single or a pair. A hand that needs a single needs the real tile, which is why those hands score higher.
items.prompt: Your hand needs one more single tile to win. Can a joker finish it?

choices: After you have already discarded that turn
When the joker is in your own exposure
When you hold two of the tile
items.explanation: Redemption happens on your turn, before you discard. Once you have thrown, the window is closed until your next turn.
items.prompt: When can you NOT redeem an exposed joker?

choices: It is against the rules to discard one
Nobody can call it, so it is safe but gone for good
It can be called for mah jongg by a player who needs a group
items.explanation: A discarded joker is dead: nobody can call it, for an exposure or for mah jongg. That makes it a safe throw, but you are giving away the most flexible tile in the set, and it tells the table you had one to spare.
items.prompt: Late in the hand, what happens to a joker you discard?

items.explanation: Only four of any tile exist, so a group of five always needs at least one joker. Most players will not commit to Quints without two.
items.prompt: How many jokers does a quint typically require?

choices: Swap your 3 Dot for their joker on your turn
items.explanation: Any exposed joker is redeemable by any player holding the tile it stands for, on their own turn. Taking an opponent's joker is one of the strongest plays in the game.
items.prompt: An opponent exposes a pung of 3 Dots using a joker. You hold a 3 Dot. What can you do?

choices: Yes, flowers in a group of three or more take jokers
Only in a pair of flowers
Only if the flowers are exposed
items.explanation: A group of three or more flowers is a group like any other, so jokers can fill it. A pair of flowers is still a pair: those two have to be real.
items.prompt: Your hand needs four flowers and you hold three. Can a joker be the fourth?

choices: No, each one is a single tile
items.explanation: Spelled one tile per digit, every digit is a single, and jokers never fill a single or a pair. Those four have to be real tiles. A digit your card shows as a pung or kong is a group like any other and does take jokers.
items.prompt: Your hand spells 2026 with one tile per digit. Can a joker stand in for one of them?
